result: Atlantic herring is one of the most abundant vertebrates with a breeding stock of one trillion individuals, has an enormous short-term effective population size but restricted long-term effective population size likely due to glaciation, and exhibits moderate nucleotide diversity (~0.3%) only three-fold higher than humans despite much larger census population size.
evaluation: Claims C1-C7 are well-supported by citations to prior published work (Feng et al., 2017; Martinez Barrio et al., 2016; Walsh and Lynch, 2018). The population size estimates, effective population size patterns, and nucleotide diversity measurements are all attributed to peer-reviewed studies, providing strong support for these background claims about Atlantic herring population genetics.

result: Atlantic herring has adapted to diverse marine environments including the brackish Baltic Sea (2-3 PSU salinity), shows minute genetic differentiation at neutral loci among populations, but exhibits significant deviation from neutral expectations with excessive outlier loci showing signatures of selection.
evaluation: Claims C8-C10 are supported by citations to prior work (Lamichhaney et al., 2012, 2017; Martinez Barrio et al., 2016; Limborg et al., 2012) and environmental data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1). The pattern of minimal neutral differentiation but excessive FST outliers is well-documented in the cited literature and forms the foundation for the current study.

result: The study performed pooled whole-genome sequencing on 28 new population samples, combined with previously published data for a total of 53 population samples covering the entire species distribution including all spawning seasons, identifying ~11.5 million polymorphic biallelic sites among Atlantic herring and ~15.9 million when including Pacific herring.
evaluation: Claims C11-C15 describe the study design and are directly supported by the Methods section and data statements. The sample sizes, sequencing approach, geographic coverage, and variant counts are clearly documented. The integration of new and published data is appropriately cited (Lamichhaney et al., 2017; Martinez Barrio et al., 2016).

result: Population structure analysis reveals seven primary clusters based on genome-wide SNPs with pairwise FST values of 0.013-0.061. PCA using 169,394 undifferentiated markers explained only ~11% variance, while PCA using 794 highly differentiated markers explained 43% variance in PC1 and separated all seven clusters, demonstrating that population structure is driven by a small fraction of markers associated with ecological adaptation.
evaluation: Claims C16-C21 are well-supported by the data presented in Figures 2, 2—figure supplement 1, and 2—figure supplement 2. The contrasting PCA results using different marker sets provide compelling evidence that population structure is driven by loci under selection rather than neutral variation. The statistical results (variance explained, FST ranges) are clearly documented and the inference about ecological adaptation (C21) is logically supported by the data.

result: Landvikvannet populations cluster with transition zone populations rather than local fjord populations, consistent with adaptation to brackish conditions. One Schlei population collected as autumn-spawning clustered with spring-spawners, and otolith examination confirmed spring hatching, demonstrating that spawning time is controlled by both genetic and environmental factors.
evaluation: Claims C22-C27 are supported by PCA data (Figure 2b), otolith examination results using established methods (Clausen et al., 2007), and citations to relevant literature (Eggers et al., 2014; McQuinn, 1997; Bekkevold et al., 2007; Berg et al., 2020). The Landvikvannet case (C22-C23) demonstrates ecological adaptation to brackish water. The Schlei case (C24-C26) provides direct empirical evidence through otolith analysis that spawning season can be plastic, supporting the conclusion about genetic and environmental control (C27).

result: Baltic/Northeast Atlantic contrasts identified 115 loci (spring-spawners) and 39 loci (autumn-spawners) reaching significance, with 30 loci significant in both comparisons. Key candidates include LRRC8C (volume-regulated anion channel) and PRLR (prolactin receptor), both highly significant in both contrasts and functionally relevant to osmoregulation and salinity adaptation.
evaluation: Claims C28-C35 are supported by genome-wide association data (Figure 3a, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 4) with stringent statistical thresholds (p<10^-10). The identification of LRRC8C and PRLR as candidates is supported by both statistical significance (p<10^-72 and p<10^-37 for LRRC8C; replicated for PRLR) and known gene functions relevant to osmoregulation (C32, C35 supported by citation to Manzon, 2002). The replication across spring and autumn spawners strengthens the inference that these loci are related to salinity adaptation rather than spawning time.

result: A large 7.8 Mb region on Chr12 shows no genetic differentiation in spring-spawning contrast but very strong differentiation between autumn-spawning Atlantic and Baltic herring, corresponding to a recently reported inversion.
evaluation: Claims C36-C37 are supported by the data in Figure 3b showing the differential pattern between spring and autumn spawners, and by citation to Pettersson et al., 2019 documenting the inversion. The spawning-season-specific differentiation pattern is clearly demonstrated in the figures and provides evidence for the functional relevance of this structural variant.

result: Spring/autumn-spawning contrasts identified 31 loci (Baltic) and 13 loci (Northeast Atlantic) with 7 replicated loci, including three within 5 Mb on Chr15. Key candidates include TSHR (thyroid-stimulating hormone receptor, p<10^-68 Baltic, p<10^-53 Atlantic), CALM1B, SOX11B (with a highly significant non-coding variant 39 kb upstream), and ESR2A/SYNE2. Multiple MYHC genes on Chr12 also show association with spawning season.
evaluation: Claims C38-C49 are well-supported by genome-wide association data (Figure 3c-d, Figure 3—figure supplement 2b, Figure 3—figure supplement 3, Supplementary file 5) with strong statistical significance. The functional relevance of candidate genes is supported by citations to relevant literature: TSHR role in seasonal reproduction (Nakane et al., 2013, 2019), CALM1B in gonadotrophin signaling (Melamed et al., 2012), SOX11B in sex determination (Santos et al., 2007), SYNE2 in photoreceptors (Maddox et al., 2015), and MYHC in seasonal development (Johnston et al., 2001). The identification of a single highly significant non-coding variant upstream of SOX11B (C46) is particularly compelling as a candidate causal regulatory mutation.

result: Ireland/Britain populations versus neighboring Northeast Atlantic populations show 12 independent loci with significant differentiation, including four major loci on Chr6, 12, 17, and 23 spanning exceptionally large regions with block-like patterns of divergence consistent with inversions. Ireland/Britain populations are predominantly homozygous for S haplotypes while N haplotypes dominate elsewhere, with the Chr6 S haplotype particularly enriched in specific Ireland/Britain spawning locations.
evaluation: Claims C50-C55 are supported by genome-wide association data (Figure 4a-e) and haplotype frequency analysis (Figure 4—figure supplements 1-3). The block-like patterns with sharp borders (C52) provide strong evidence for structural variants (C53), consistent with suppressed recombination. The geographic distribution of haplotypes (C54-C55) is clearly documented and supports the inference of local adaptation. The pattern differs from typical selective sweeps, strengthening the structural variant hypothesis.

result: The Chr12 inversion is potentially associated with adaptation to water temperature at spawning or larval stage, with recombinant versions frequent in the Baltic Sea showing variable breakpoints.
evaluation: Claims C56-C57 are supported by citations to recent studies (Pettersson et al., 2019; Fuentes-Pardo et al., 2019) and individual sequence data showing recombinant haplotypes (Figure 4—figure supplement 2). The temperature association hypothesis is supported by prior work, and the detection of recombinants with variable breakpoints demonstrates incomplete recombination suppression and provides insight into the evolutionary dynamics of this inversion.

result: Both N and S haplotypes at the four putative inversion loci show lower nucleotide diversity (0.11-0.31%) than the genome average (~0.3%), with S haplotypes more variable than N haplotypes, suggesting restricted recombination between haplotypes and that N haplotypes are younger or more affected by bottlenecks.
evaluation: Claims C58-C60 are supported by nucleotide diversity analysis (Figure 4—figure supplement 4). The reduced diversity within haplotypes (C58) is consistent with suppressed recombination. The pattern of higher diversity in S versus N haplotypes (C59) supports the inference that N haplotypes are derived (C60), though alternative explanations (differential bottleneck effects) are appropriately acknowledged. The data are consistent with the hypothesis but do not definitively prove the evolutionary scenario.

result: The most striking signal in North Atlantic herring is a locus on Chr2 overlapping AHR2B2, with four of ten top SNPs being missense mutations. The Ser346Thr mutation shows the strongest differentiation (p<10^-45) and is likely causal, with Thr346 at high frequency in North Atlantic populations and Ser346 dominating elsewhere.
evaluation: Claims C61-C64 are strongly supported by genome-wide association data (Figure 5a-b) and allele frequency analysis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a). The statistical significance is exceptional (p<10^-45), and the presence of multiple missense mutations with Ser346Thr showing by far the strongest signal (C62) provides compelling evidence for a causal variant (C63). The geographic distribution of alleles (C64) is clearly documented and consistent with adaptation in North Atlantic populations.

result: Additional significant loci in North Atlantic herring include a SNP ~1 kb upstream of SLA12A2/NKCC1 (p<10^-24), a gene showing altered expression in response to salinity changes in sea lamprey, and THRB on Chr19, where mutations cause thyroid hormone resistance in humans and affect photoreceptor development in zebrafish.
evaluation: Claims C65-C68 are supported by genome-wide association data (Figure 5a) and citations to relevant functional studies (Ferreira-Martins et al., 2016 for SLA12A2/NKCC1; Ferrara et al., 2012 and Deveau et al., 2019 for THRB). The functional relevance of these genes to osmoregulation and photoperiod regulation provides biological plausibility for their roles in ecological adaptation, though direct functional validation in herring is not provided.

result: At the THRB locus, all high-salinity populations are fixed for an Atlantic haplotype, while a 'Baltic' haplotype dominates in Baltic Sea, transition zone, and Norwegian fjord populations. This Baltic haplotype must have been introgressed from Pacific herring and differs by only a single missense mutation (Gln40His) from the Pacific herring haplotype.
evaluation: Claims C69-C71 are supported by haplotype frequency data (Figure 5—figure supplement 2) and sequence comparison. The geographic distribution pattern (C69) is clearly documented. The inference of introgression from Pacific herring (C70) is strongly supported by the near-identity of the Baltic haplotype to Pacific herring, differing by only one missense mutation (C71). This represents compelling evidence for adaptive introgression, though the functional significance of the Gln40His mutation is not directly tested.

result: PacBio long-read sequencing provided conclusive evidence for inversions on Chr6 (breakpoints at 24,868,581 bp and 22,280,036-22,290,000 bp) and Chr17 (breakpoints at 25,805,445 bp and 27,568,511 bp). The Chr17 inversion includes a 5 kb duplicated sequence in the N haplotype present as single copy in the S haplotype, indicating N is the derived state and that inversion and duplication occurred in the same meiotic event.
evaluation: Claims C72-C79 are strongly supported by PacBio long-read sequencing data (Figure 6) with multiple supporting reads (34 for Chr6, 36 for Chr17). The precise breakpoint mapping (C73-C75) provides conclusive structural evidence. The duplication pattern at Chr17 (C76-C77) provides strong evidence that N is derived (C78) and that inversion and duplication occurred together (C79), as this is the most parsimonious explanation. This represents high-quality structural variant validation using appropriate long-read technology.

result: The Chr6 and Chr17 inversions contain 44 and 66 genes respectively. Inversion breakpoints do not disrupt coding sequences, but the Chr6 proximal breakpoint is located very close to exon 1 of PRMT3, a highly conserved gene involved in bone development in humans, suggesting potential effects on expression.
evaluation: Claims C80-C84 are supported by gene annotation of the inverted regions and PacBio sequencing data (Figure 6). The gene counts (C80-C81) are straightforward to determine from the reference assembly. The observation that breakpoints do not disrupt coding sequences (C82) is conclusively demonstrated for Chr6 and Chr17. The proximity of the Chr6 breakpoint to PRMT3 (C83) is documented, and the gene's conservation and function (C84, supported by Min et al., 2019) provide biological plausibility for regulatory effects, though this remains speculative.

result: Early population genetic studies using allozyme markers found no significant differentiation between Atlantic and Baltic herring. The current study demonstrates that sequence variants associated with ecological adaptation best reveal population structure, with ~800 SNPs distinguishing all major groups. Single markers like Ser346Thr in AHR can efficiently distinguish North Atlantic from other herring groups.
evaluation: Claims C85-C88 are well-supported. C85 is supported by citations to early studies (Andersson et al., 1981; Ryman et al., 1984). C86-C87 are supported by the PCA results (Figure 2a vs 2b) demonstrating the superior discriminatory power of selected markers. C88 is supported by allele frequency data (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a) showing clear geographic differentiation at this single locus. This represents an important practical application of the findings for fisheries management.

result: The genetic architecture underlying ecological adaptation in Atlantic herring is polygenic with hundreds (not thousands) of loci showing strong differentiation, deviating from the infinitesimal model which predicts only minor allele frequency changes. This architecture is similar to human skin color, where four major loci explain 35% of variance, and reflects adaptation over many generations including to the Baltic Sea formed ~10,000 years ago.
evaluation: Claims C89-C92 are supported by the study's findings and appropriate comparisons. C89 is directly supported by the hundreds of significant loci identified across contrasts. C90 correctly notes the deviation from infinitesimal model predictions based on the large allele frequency shifts observed. C91 is supported by citation to Andrén et al., 2011 for Baltic Sea formation. C92 provides an appropriate comparison to human skin color (Beleza et al., 2013) as an example of strong selection. The reasoning is sound, though the comparison between standing variation in human GWAS and herring adaptation over evolutionary time (noted in the text) is important context.

result: A missense mutation in rhodopsin (Phe261Tyr) has a critical role for adaptation to red-shifted light conditions in the Baltic Sea, with about one-third of all fish adapted to red-shifted light in freshwater and brackish water carrying Tyr261, representing convergent evolution.
evaluation: Claims C93-C94 are supported by citation to Hill et al., 2019 and reference to Figure 3a showing genetic differentiation at RHO. The functional role of Phe261Tyr in light adaptation (C93) and the convergent evolution pattern (C94) are both attributed to the cited study. This represents an important example of a likely causal mutation with clear functional significance, though the current manuscript does not provide new functional data on this locus.

result: Thr346 is the derived allele at AHR2B2 since all Pacific herring were homozygous Ser346. Residue 346 is located in the highly conserved PAS-B domain and Ser346 is highly conserved among vertebrates, suggesting functional significance of the Ser346Thr mutation.
evaluation: Claims C95-C97 are supported by comparative sequence data and conservation analysis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1b). The inference that Thr346 is derived (C95) is strongly supported by the Pacific herring data, as the sister species provides an appropriate outgroup. The location in the PAS-B domain (C96) and conservation of Ser346 across vertebrates (C97) are documented in the alignment and provide strong evidence for functional constraint, making the Ser346Thr substitution particularly notable.

result: While killifish adapted to polluted waters via AHR deletion, the derived Thr346 allele in herring occurs at high frequency in the least polluted North Atlantic waters (e.g., Greenland, Iceland), with billions of herring homozygous for Thr346, suggesting adaptation is not related to exogenous metabolites.
evaluation: Claims C98-C100 are supported by citation to Oziolor et al., 2019 for the killifish case (C98) and allele frequency data (Figure 5—figure supplement 1b) for herring (C99-C100). The reasoning that high Thr346 frequency in pristine waters argues against pollution-related adaptation (C99) is logical, though not definitive. The statement about billions of homozygous herring (C100) is consistent with the population size data and allele frequencies. The contrast with killifish effectively rules out one hypothesis while leaving the actual selective pressure uncertain.

result: The four inversion polymorphisms on Chr6, 12, 17, and 23 share characteristic features: breakpoints do not disrupt coding sequences (conclusive for Chr6 and 17), no allele is lethal when homozygous, inversions suppress but do not completely prevent recombination, and none are of recent origin (nucleotide diversity 0.11-0.31% within haplotypes). Strong genetic differentiation among populations implies these are supergenes important for environmental adaptation.
evaluation: Claims C101-C105 are well-supported by multiple lines of evidence. C101 is conclusively demonstrated for Chr6 and Chr17 by PacBio data (Figure 6). C102 is inferred from observation of homozygous individuals in the data. C103 is supported by evidence of recombinant haplotypes (Figure 4—figure supplement 2). C104 is supported by nucleotide diversity analysis (Figure 4—figure supplement 4). C105 is supported by strong population differentiation (Figure 4—figure supplement 3). Together, these characteristics define these inversions as balanced polymorphisms maintained by selection, representing supergenes for ecological adaptation.

result: Ecological adaptation in Atlantic herring is associated with large shifts in allele frequencies at loci under selection.
evaluation: Claim C106 represents the main conclusion of the study and is strongly supported by the comprehensive genome-wide association analyses showing hundreds of loci with large allele frequency differences (often approaching fixation) between ecologically distinct populations. The delta allele frequency distributions (e.g., Figure 3—figure supplement 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 3) clearly demonstrate large shifts at loci above the significance threshold, contrasting with the small shifts expected under an infinitesimal model.
